newsitem.title: USA: Albright to face domestic-oriented U.S. Congress.
newsitem.headline: Albright to face domestic-oriented U.S. Congress.

text.p: The United States will soon have a new secretary of state, but nominee Madeleine Albright, if confirmed, will face a U.S. body politic focused more than ever on domestic problems rather than foreign crises.

Senate confirmation hearing on Wednesday for Albright showed only limited interest among legislators in such issues as promoting the Middle East peace process, expanding NATO or managing relations with Russia.

Instead, the questions that dominated the hearing before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee reflected home-grown concerns: holding down foreign spending, stemming the influx of drugs and keeping U.S. troops out of foreign wars.

The tone of the hearing demonstrated how far the tide has turned in the United States against foreign entanglements since the end of the Cold War, and the extent to which the administration has come to terms with the new mood.

In her address to the committee, Albright warned against trends towards isolationism. "We must be more than audience, more even than actors, we must be the authors of the history of our age," she said.

Her presentation made clear that a growing concern in the administration is how it can persuade the American public that it needs to bother about foreign policy. "It matters...", she began six consecutive sentences.

But Albright, whose printed text contained proposals for reviving peace talks on Cyprus and Nagorno-Karabakh, omitted these sections in her oral presentation, apparently sensing they were of secondary interest to the committee.

Albright, set to take over as secretary of state on Jan. 20 from Warren Christopher, concentrated instead on the need for adequate State Department funding and efforts to secure a better deal for American business in world markets.
Her focus implicitly reflected the agenda set by the majority Republicans on the committee and its conservative chairman, Jesse Helms of North Carolina.

In an introductory speech, Helms listed as his priorities: streamlining the "antiquated" U.S. foreign policy bureaucracy; reforming the United Nations; ensuring that U.S. troops are not sent abroad without a clear mission; and tightening surveillance of foreign aid programmes.

In an obvious message to Albright, Washington's outgoing U.N. ambassador, the committee had posted a chart in the hearing room showing a convoluted diagram of the scores of U.N. bodies, committees and agencies under the headline "The United Nations: One Big Mess".

Albright said she was "open-minded" on U.S. foreign policy restructuring, a proposal hitherto rejected by the Clinton administration that would involve folding three independent agencies into the State Department.
She expressed support for U.N. reform but stressed the need for the United States to clear outstanding arrears to the world body, whose payment has been held up by Congress.

Democrats on the committee appeared as focused on domestic issues as their Republican colleagues, with several calling for pressure on Mexico and other Latin American countries to crack down harder on drug smuggling into the United States.
Joseph Biden of Delaware, senior Democrat on the committee, amended President Bill Clinton's 1992 campaign motto "It's the economy, stupid."
"I'm here to tell you it's drugs, stupid, it's drugs. It's drugs. It's drugs. It's drugs," he said.
